log: The `transports` slot was classified `never` and filed with `clients` under live connections, as if it held network `Transport`s. It is the unit `TransportRegistry`: one `TransportManifest` per unit aboard a ship or Carrier. So no save carried them, and `gameForLoad` adopted the running game's registry instead of a fresh one. In-process that hid the loss behind manifests pointing at the pre-save units; after a real reload every stowed unit was aboard nothing.

It is now `state`, and `TransportManifest` (a `DataObject` from `core-unit-transport@0.1.9`) is in `CORE_ENTITIES` so a save can name it. web-renderer's `test:save` now lands a Fighter on a Carrier before saving and checks it is still aboard, and still `Stowed`, after loading.

`core-save-game` discovers entities by walking `DataObject`s, and a manifest was a plain class, so no save carried one. A loaded game had every unit aboard a ship or Carrier still marked `Stowed` but aboard nothing: the ship sailed without it, and an aircraft was lost at its next fuel check. `StrategyNote` went through the same change.

It now extends `DataObject` with `sourceTile`, `transport` and `unit` as keys, all entities, so they are saved as `$ref`s and restored as the loaded instances. The constructor signature is unchanged. Only the first finger pans the map. Touching or lifting another no longer stops a glide, ends the drag or counts as a tap on the tile under it.

Press and drag anywhere on the map to pan it; let go mid-drag and it glides to a stop, and pressing again catches it. A quick click still centres on a tile or opens a city or unit, and a long press still opens the unit's actions.

W (wait) is meant to put a unit to one side and come back to it once everything else has moved, but it only ever flicked to the next unit, and the one you skipped could turn straight back up. A unit you wait now goes to the back of the queue and returns after every other unit has had its turn, longest-waiting first. Waiting your last unit simply keeps it selected (#10).

F5 was handled by two keydown listeners: the reload guard (fires everywhere) and the leader-screens map (fires once a game is running, opening TradeReport), so in-game F5 showed both. The reload guard now only claims F5 before a game starts; Ctrl/Cmd+R still always confirms a reload (#10).

W was mapped to a non-existent 'Wait' unit action, so it always fell through to a plain cycle to the next active unit, and the unit was never deferred. W now sends the current unit to the back of a queue: waited units (tracked by id, since every update reconstitutes fresh objects) are held out of auto-selection until every other active unit has had its turn, then come back longest-waiting first. When everything else is already waiting, W wraps round to the longest-waiting unit; with a single active unit it keeps that unit selected (#10).

The map used to hold a full-size copy of the whole world for every layer it draws — seven of them, over a hundred and thirty megabytes before a single tile appears, and more again on a bigger map. Each layer is now only as big as the window you are looking through, which hands back about ninety-five megabytes and stops the cost growing with the map (#7).

It redraws only the part of the screen that actually changed, too. Scrolling moves the picture it already has and fills in the strip coming into view, and the unit waiting for orders blinks by repainting its own tile instead of the entire map.
Resizing the window could leave the map blank until something else happened to redraw it. It comes straight back now.

Every layer was a canvas the size of the whole world — 2560x1920 at 80x60 scale 2, and seven of them, 137.4 MB before a tile is drawn, growing with the map. A layer is now the size of the portal that composites it, with `#originX` and `#originY` saying which world pixel sits at its top left corner: 40.0 MB for the same world, and a world twice the size costs the same again.

That means a tile no longer has one fixed place on a canvas, and because the world wraps it can have several places or none. Layers are handed the places to draw in rather than working them out from the tile's co-ordinates — `drawTile(tile, offsetX, offsetY)`, called once per place — so `Portal` has no wrap offsets to composite any more, and the overflow `CityNames` used to draw a canvas-width away to survive being tiled is now just another placement. Moving the view blits the overlap across and draws only the strips it uncovers.

Layers record what they changed, and `Portal.render()` composites those regions rather than the whole canvas, which is what restricting the blink tick to the active unit's region needed: `ActiveUnit` is the topmost layer, so un-drawing it means restoring the pixels beneath it. A blink composite is 0.006 megapixels and 5.5 `drawImage` calls against 10.5 and 7 for a full one. Regions are unioned until none overlap, because compositing a pixel twice doubles up anything drawn with alpha, and past half the canvas or eight regions it composites the lot instead. What a tile draws past its own square is recorded as it is drawn rather than declared per layer, so the city glyph, a yield icon and the copy behind a stack all reach the composite without the sprite sizes being second-guessed.

Verified in the browser on an 80x60 world at scale 2 in a 1712x873 portal: after panning, city windows, overlay toggles and blinks the incrementally composited portal is pixel-identical to a full composite, and a viewport reached by short scrolling hops is pixel-identical to the same viewport drawn from nothing — 0 of 1,494,576 pixels differ in each case. The geometry underneath is exhaustively tested offline.

Fixed on the way: the resize handler assigned `mapPortal.width` and `height` unconditionally, and assigning either clears a canvas even when the value has not changed. A resize that resized nothing therefore wiped the map, and with the portal compositing only what changed it put nothing back.

The map used to build its scenery on six separate world-sized canvases and stack them up on every redraw, then composite every one of them at every wrapped position — including positions entirely off the screen. It draws the same picture from one canvas now, and only over the part of the screen it actually covers: sixty draws and nearly three hundred megapixels a frame down to fifteen and seven and a half, and about ninety megabytes of memory handed back (#7).

The minimap turned out to be the more expensive half, once the map stopped drowning it out. It made its picture by shrinking three full-size copies of the world down to a couple of hundred pixels across, every time anything changed. It has a small picture of its own now, drawn at the size it is actually shown: terrain in flat colours, cities in their owner's colour so you can see whose land is whose, and nothing at all where you have not been yet (#53).

The unit waiting for orders shows there as a flashing white tile, so you can find it at a glance and click straight to it. Clicking takes you where you clicked, too — it used to land two tiles up and to the left (#54).

The minimap is drawn at a whole number of pixels per tile and scaled up, rather than squeezed down to a fractional size, so it is sharp for the first time. And the box showing the part of the world you are looking at comes back round the other side when the map wraps, instead of running off the edge and leaving half of itself behind.

`Minimap.update()` composited by scaling three full-world canvases down to 190px wide — 14.7 megapixels thrown away on every patch and every recentre. Over 15s of stress play that was 383.4 megapixels against the portal's 310.9, so the minimap had quietly become the larger consumer of the two. It draws from an `Overview` layer rendered at a few pixels a tile now: 0.79 megapixels over the same window, and one blit an update rather than three. A tile change repaints one tile instead of the world.

The overview draws terrain as one flat colour per type, cities in the owner's colour so rival territory can be read at a glance, and nothing at all for unexplored, so how much of the world is still dark stays legible. Terrains come from a registry plugins extend, so anything the colour table does not know falls back to land or water rather than leaving a hole. It deliberately ignores the layers' `isVisible()`: hiding yields or units is a view mode for the map, not for an overview.

The active unit is a white tile that flashes in time with the main map, so it can be found on the minimap and clicked to centre without reaching for the keyboard. Flashing means redrawing the minimap twice a second, which is only affordable now the layer is small.
The minimap is rendered at a whole number of pixels a tile and upscaled by CSS rather than drawn at a fractional size, so the tiles are finally crisp.

Clicking it now centres where you clicked. `event.offsetX` is already relative to the canvas but the handler subtracted the element's `offsetLeft` as well, and `Math.ceil` should have been `Math.floor`, which together landed the map two tiles up and left of the click.

The world wraps but the box showing what the portal is looking at did not, so centring near an edge drew it running off that side with nothing coming back on the opposite one — a viewport that was plainly half missing. `rawVisibleRange()` is unwrapped by design, so the box is now drawn from its wrapped origin and again a world earlier on whichever axis overflows. The copies' outer edges fall off the canvas, so the two halves meet without a seam. This was the `TODO: draw the rectangle replicated when close to the sides` that sat on the old rect.
Both edges are floored now rather than the width being floored on its own, so a box covers the same tiles however it is split.

Scoping the viewport-buffer work turned up that `Minimap.update()` is the renderer's largest source-pixel consumer: it discards 14.7 megapixels into a 190x142 target on every patch and every recentre, 383.4 megapixels over 15s of stress play against the portal's 310.9. It is also the whole of the blocker on viewport-sized buffers, being the only thing outside `Portal` that reads a layer's `canvas()`. Filed as #53 with the decisions on what a dedicated minimap layer draws, and #54 for the click landing two tiles up and left of the tile clicked.

The six layers that draw a tile's own scenery — land and coast, irrigation, terrain, improvements, terrain features and goody huts — were six world-sized canvases the portal composited in order on every render. Nothing ever toggled any of them on its own and they only change when a tile changes, so they are one `Landscape` canvas now, drawn in the same order. The main portal holds seven world canvases instead of twelve, and the city portal six instead of ten; the city map gains goody huts, which it had been the only portal not to draw.

`Portal.render()` drew every layer at every wrapped offset as a full-layer blit, including offsets that fell entirely off the canvas. It works out once, for all the layers, which repeats land on the canvas and which part of each one does. On an 80x60 world at scale 2 in a 1712x873 portal that takes a render from 60.5 `drawImage` calls and 297 megapixels of source down to 15.0 calls and 7.5 megapixels.
The marker for a road with no neighbouring road called `rect()` and `fill()` without a `beginPath()`, so every marker re-filled every isolated road drawn before it. It begins a path now.
Importing SP257.PIC and TER257.PIC used to lock the page up for well over two minutes. It now finishes in about a quarter of a second, and the page stays responsive while it does (#50).

The work was one loop: knocking the transparent colour out of each sprite read the canvas a single pixel at a time, and swept the whole 320x200 source image rather than the sprite sitting in the corner of it — eighteen million reads to handle sixty-nine thousand pixels. The extracted sprites are unchanged, right down to the pixel. Writing them to the browser's database is one transaction now rather than one per sprite, and the dialog no longer warns you to go and make a cup of tea.

`pnpm update @civ-clone/civ1-asset-extractor` repoints the lockfile from ee19340 to 4860507, which is the per-sprite `getImageData` rewrite the previous commit measured. The renderer consumed the extractor straight from its default branch, so the import stayed slow until the lockfile moved.

log: The transparency pass called `getImageData(x, y, 1, 1)` once per pixel, and looped over the 320x200 source canvas rather than the sprite's own bounds, so ~99.6% of the iterations read outside the sprite and did nothing. Across the 286 sprites in `extract-data.json` that is 18,304,002 readbacks to process 69,194 pixels.

One `getImageData` over the sprite, a walk of the buffer zeroing matching pixels, and one `putImageData` does the same job in 288 readbacks. Verified pixel-identical output for all 286 sprites from `TER257.PIC` and `SP257.PIC`.

Eleven of the entries in this window were blank, including one for every release: a commit written as a subject with no body had that subject mistaken for a `Co-Authored-By:`-style trailer and thrown away. They have their text back, and an entry with nothing in it is no longer shown at all.
The end-of-turn button now dims and stops responding the moment it is pressed, rather than sitting there inviting a second press that would send the turn twice.

Closes #11. `activate()` set `disabled` on `element()`, which is the wrapping `.action` div, and the attribute means nothing on a div: the button neither disabled nor dimmed, and both the click handler and the keyboard handler in `Actions` would call `activate()` again and send a second `EndTurn` to the engine.

It now disables the `button` itself and returns early when it is already disabled, so the turn ends once. `.action button:disabled` dims it and stops the end-of-turn glow, and the next turn's actions arrive as a freshly built `EndTurn`, so it comes back enabled on its own.

Verified in the browser: on press the button reports `disabled`, `grayscale(0.7) brightness(0.6)` and no `::before` animation, and the next turn's panel has an enabled one again. The `img` tag in `build()` was also missing its closing `>`.

Closes #51. `toBullets` tested every line of a single-paragraph message against `TRAILER`, and `/^[A-Za-z][\w-]*: \S/` matches `release: …` and `docs: …` exactly as it matches `Co-Authored-By: …`. `renderActiveUnit` re-rendered the entire `Units` layer on every unit selection and every unit move: a full-canvas clear plus a `renderTile` for every tile in the world, measured at 1,207 per-tile clears for a single unit move (#47).

`AssetStore.getImage` created a detached ``, set `src`, and returned it without waiting. A detached element is never rendered, so its intrinsic size is 0 until it loads -- and `scaleImage` sized its canvas from `image.width`. The result was a 0x0 canvas, which `getScaled` then cached permanently under that path, so any icon that lost the race stayed blank for the rest of the session and `toDataURL()` handed consumers `"data:,"`.

`getImage` waits for the `load` event before caching, and leaves a failed image uncached so a later import can replace it. Deliberately not `decode()`: for an element that is not in the document, `decode()` never settles while the page is hidden, and this is awaited during init, so it stopped the app starting at all in a background tab.
`scaleImage` sizes from `imageSize` and returns a 1x1 rather than a default-sized canvas for a source with no dimensions, which consumers would otherwise embed as a visibly empty 300x150 box.
`getScaled` keys on the scale as well as the path. Keying on the path alone served the first scale asked for to every later caller; every call site uses 2 today, so this was latent.

Verified with a real asset import -- init reliable over four consecutive loads with the document hidden, the cursor correct, and the City details report's scaled yield icons all rendering at 14x14 with none blank.

`getPreloadedImage` returned `image.cloneNode()` on every lookup. A clone is detached, so it is neither rendered nor decoded and its `width` reads 0 on first use -- which `replaceColours` fed straight into `getImageData` as a zero-sized rect, throwing `IndexSizeError` the first time a unit image was used (the city build header) (#8). Return the preloaded element itself and size from `naturalWidth`/ `naturalHeight`, which the `#preload` originals report correctly because the container clips them rather than hiding them. `replaceColours` and `Map.putImage` now bail out on a source with no dimensions instead of throwing, since the preload is asynchronous and an early render can arrive first.
With the clone gone the derived canvases can be cached rather than rebuilt:
`replaceColours` returns its cache entry directly instead of cloning it per hit, and keys on the source colours too -- the same sprite recoloured from a different source set is a different result.
`renderUnit` caches the fully rendered unit, keyed on type, colours, fortified and busy state, and composites the overlays onto its own canvas so it never draws on the shared recolour entry.
`Map/Land` caches the composed coast tile by its 8-neighbour bitmask, which bounds it at 256 small canvases instead of one per coast tile per render.
A cache entry is skipped whenever it would be built from an image that had not decoded, so a missing sprite cannot stick for the session, and all three drop when the preload container changes.

Verified against a real asset import (TER257.PIC/SP257.PIC) with the stress harness: 171 turns, no render errors, no zero-sized `getImageData`, and `getImageData` calls -- one per recolour cache miss -- flat at 6 to 12 across the run rather than one per unit per render.

hydrate restores a cycle without running a constructor, loads a format-1 file still carrying the old empty placeholder, and a re-save is byte-identical.

log: Same gap as `Sleeping`: `BusyRegistry` listed `Stowed` among the states a lookup covers and nothing registered it, so a unit saved aboard a transport failed to load.

`Stowed`'s criterion is `() => false` — it never clears itself; disembarking replaces the busy rule instead. So there is nothing to reconstruct and the factory is the constructor. What keeps the unit on the transport is ordinary saved state on the transport, not this rule.

The last `Busy` state with no way to be rebuilt after a load. It could not be registered before, because the path its criterion compares against was never written to the file — `StrategyNote` was not a `DataObject`, so nothing in `strategyNotes` was saved — and inventing a path on load would have sent the unit somewhere it had not been going.
Two changes make the rule reconstructible:

The note holds the remaining `Tile`s rather than the `Path`. A note is saved state now, and `encode` writes a registry held as a field as an array of its members without recording the class, so a stored `Path` would come back as a plain array with no `end()`. Everything the journey needs is `shift()`, `length` and "the last one", which an array does natively and symmetrically across a save — `moveAlongPath` only ever used the first two. `entries()` returns a copy, so the array is ours to consume.

And the criterion reads the note each time instead of closing over the path, which is what leaves nothing in the rule but the unit. It also covers the note being gone — which happens the moment the unit arrives and `moveAlongPath` unregisters it — so no note means the journey is over and the unit wakes. `Rules/Player/turn-start` already recovered that way at runtime; the rule now agrees with it.

Verified in web-renderer's save suite against a real 12-turn game: a unit put on a journey comes back still following it, the tiles come back as `Tile`s rather than `$ref` strings, ending where they ended before, and the rebuilt rule reports the journey unfinished. The round trip stays byte-identical.

`Pillage` extends `DelayedAction` and was still passing a completion callback to `super.perform`, which now takes a handler identifier. Four consumers stop compiling — `library-unit`, `simple-ai-client`, `simple-world-path` and `civ1-unit` — and at runtime a pillaging unit would register a `PendingEffect` whose handler is a stringified closure, then throw `UnknownHandlerError` when it came due.

It was missed because the grep meant to find every `DelayedAction` subclass searched `node_modules/@civ-clone/*`, which are symlinks into pnpm's store — `grep -r` does not follow symlinks and returned nothing at all. `grep -R` finds eleven, not nine. `Fortify` was missed the same way and found by the same runtime error.

`Pillaging` is new. This action had no `Busy` subclass and used the base `Busy`, which cannot go in `BusyRegistry`: it is keyed by type name, so registering the base would claim the identity for every state that never subclassed it.

`BusyRegistry` named `Sleeping` among the states a lookup covers, but nothing ever registered it. A unit saved asleep therefore failed to load with `UnknownBusyError` — correct behaviour over guessing, but the gap was mine and not the registry's.

Nothing in the rule came from the action: the criterion is "an enemy is visible from where I am" and the effect is "wake up", both read off the unit and the world. Building it inline in `perform`, closing over `this.from()` and the action's own registry, made it look like it held action state. It never did, so `sleeping(unit)` builds it the same way fresh or restored.
`Sleep` extends `DelayedAction` but never calls `super.perform`, so it owes nothing and needs no `PendingEffect` — a plain factory is the whole story.

The grant used to be a one-shot rule registered inside an `Effect`, which registered another one-shot rule, each closing over the `PlayerResearch` it applied to. A closure cannot be written to a file, so a save taken between finishing the wonder and starting the next research lost the two free advances silently — the player never got them and nothing said why.

`building-complete.test.ts` covers the grant. This covers the reason it was rebuilt on `PendingEffect`: that what records the debt now reaches the file, comes back pointing at the restored research, and is still spendable.

Written in web-renderer first, because `core-pending-effect` was unpublished and this package could not install. It belongs here, and it needs no world, no plugin loader and no seeded game to make its point.

The player is deliberately left out of `game.players`: it has no civilisation, and `hydrate`'s claim-replaying pass reads one from every player in that registry. A player without one cannot occur in a real game — `civ1-player` assigns a civilisation as the player is created — so hardening that pass would only hide a genuinely broken save.

`01-constraints.md` §4's one unserialisable continuation. It granted two free research completions by registering a one-shot rule that registered another one-shot rule, each closing over the `PlayerResearch` it applied to — so the only record of the grant was a closure in the rule registry, and a save taken between finishing the wonder and starting the next research lost it silently. The player simply never got their advances.

What records it now is a `PendingEffect` against the player's research: "owed two completions". The rule that spends them, `Rules/PlayerResearch/started`, is registered at import like every other rule — which is also why this stops needing `ruleRegistry.register` inside an `Effect`, the pattern Stage 6 adds a lint rule against.

Partly-paid debts write the remainder back rather than discharging, because discharging forgets — and a save taken between the first completion and the second would then lose the second. The last one discharges, which removes the debt and applies it.

The test for the grant now registers the rule it depends on, which it could not before: the rule did not exist until the wonder's effect created it. That is the same lesson `civ1-city`'s suite taught — a test should declare every input it relies on.

Verified end to end in the renderer: 9/9 in `npm run test:darwins`, and the conformance checksums are unchanged. The rule-count instrument moved from 1,055 to 1,056 with `Started` going 1 → 2, which is exactly right: one permanent rule at import in place of one-shots at runtime.

A `pendingEffects` slot, per-game like everything else. It holds what the game owes its entities — a unit part-way through building a road, a player owed free research — as saveable records rather than closures.

`Game` holds a `pendingEffects` slot, so its own tests could not run until that package was published — which is why the publish gate stopped here rather than half-publishing the wave. This package tracks its lockfile, so the resolution is part of the commit.
The engine has two unserialisable continuations and they looked like separate problems:

**A delayed action.** `DelayedAction.perform` closes over `endTurn = turn.value() + turns` and a completion callback, so a unit three turns into building a road holds its remaining work entirely in a closure.
**Darwin's Voyage.** It grants two free research completions by registering a one-shot rule that registers another one-shot rule, each closing over the `PlayerResearch` it applies to.

Both are the same thing: a **debt owed to a target entity**. "This unit is owed the completion of a road at turn 41." "This player's research is owed two free completions." The closures implement the debt; only the debt needs saving. `01-constraints.md` §4 took Darwin's Voyage to be the engine's one unserialisable continuation — it is one of nine, since eight unit actions go through `DelayedAction`.

**There is deliberately no trigger.** Modelling *when* an effect is due — a turn, an event, a condition — is the obvious next move and the wrong one: it would be a second, weaker scheduler beside the one the engine already has. A package registers an ordinary rule, once at import, that watches whatever it cares about and discharges the effects that have come due. Leaving timing out is exactly what lets one class cover both cases:
build road       …build-road:complete   Unit            endTurn     the Busy criterion Darwin's Voyage  civ1-wonder:darwins…   PlayerResearch  remaining   a Started rule

`handler` is a string so the closure stays in the plugin and the file holds only a name. `target` is a `DataObject` so it saves as a `$ref` and comes back as the restored instance — typed as the base class, because a debt is owed to a `Unit`, a `PlayerResearch` or anything else and nothing here needs to know which.

`discharge` unregisters *before* applying, and the test says why twice over: a handler that owes a follow-up must not have it removed by the discharge that caused it, and an effect whose handler throws must not be retried every turn for ever.

`DataObject` declares `_keys: (keyof this)[]`, and that polymorphic `this` makes no subclass assignable to the base — passing a `Unit` fails on `'player' is not assignable to keyof DataObject`. The public interface says everything this needs and has no such problem.
Stage 6 of the engine serialisation plan, and the answer to 02-design-review.md §3: "208 `Rule` subclasses exist across the tree. Not one rule instance has a name, an id, or a declared origin."
`Rule`'s constructor now accepts a leading string. It is optional, so this lands package by package and the 1,055 rules a real game registers keep working untouched.

**Strings rather than subclasses, and the numbers decide it.** A real game registers 1,055 rule *instances* across 163 classes. Naming an instance is the thing `replace`, `disable`, `before` and `after` need, and no amount of subclassing provides it — you cannot subclass 1,055 times, and the second instance of any class is unaddressable either way. Subclasses answer "what kind of rule is this", which the engine already has and already uses well.

**`before`/`after` reposition rather than compute a priority.** Giving a rule `target.priority() - 1` looks simpler and is wrong twice: `Normal` is 2000 for almost everything, so "one less" collides with whatever else sits there, and it breaks silently when the target's priority later changes. Position is what `before` means, so position is what gets set — after the existing priority sort, which `Array.prototype.sort` keeps stable. Rules with no constraint take an early return, so the hot path is exactly as cheap as before.

**Every id-taking method throws on an unknown id.** A plugin that means to replace `civ1-city:city/grow` and mistypes it should fail at load, not run a game where its override silently never applied — which is the failure mode strings invite and the reason to guard it. Two rules claiming one id is refused at registration for the same reason `ClassRegistry` refuses two classes: the loser would be unaddressable.

The test for two rules constrained against one target caught a real bug: inserting each at `index + 1` made the second land before the first, so they came out reversed. They are grouped and spliced as a unit now, with priority deciding within a group.

The publish gate reported it: "a forced rebuild reformats 3 file(s); the commit is what gets published". The emitted `.js` and its map described the pre-prettier source, because this package was built before the format-compile-format ordering was applied to it — the same drift that 23 of Stage 4's commits carried, and that `lib/procedure.js` and `tools/stage4.js` were both changed to prevent.

Behaviour is identical either way; the artifact simply did not match the `.ts` beside it, which is exactly the kind of thing that survives every gate. A second format-compile-format pass now changes nothing.

**A real game now saves and loads byte-identically.** Turn 12 of the conformance game: 6,499 entities, 23 registries, 57KB gzipped; saved, loaded into a fresh game, saved again, and the two files are identical. That is the check that catches a dropped field, and it passes.

`pendingEffects` is a saved registry. The debts are entities; the handlers that discharge them are functions registered at import and are never saved, which is the whole point — a closure cannot be written to a file.

`Unit._busy` encodes as `{ $busy: '<class>' }`. It is the only field in the engine that holds a `Rule` — measured: 1,055 registered rules, 4,007 reachable entities, two fields. A rule is a closure, but *which* rule is a name, and every `Busy` subclass carries no instance state: anything that varies, like when a delayed action finishes, now lives in a `PendingEffect`.

`hydrate` resolves those markers in a pass of its own, after the fill. Rebuilding one needs the entity that holds it, and `decode` walks a field's value with no idea whose field it is. The order matters: the pending effects are filled by the pass before, so a factory asking when a road finishes can read it.
`$busy` is a distinct marker rather than a `$class` because a class reference decodes to the class, and what a unit needs back is an *instance*, built for it by the package that owns it.
`test:save` is wired into `npm test` now that it passes, and the registry-membership assertion compares a summary rather than printing several thousand ids on every run.

`Unit._busy` is the only field in the engine that holds a `Rule` — measured: 1,055 registered rules, 4,007 reachable entities, exactly two fields, both `<Unit>._busy`. A rule is a closure, so `core-save-game` refuses to encode one, and that single field is what blocks saving.

`BusyRegistry` maps a `Busy` identity to a factory that rebuilds it for a unit. A factory rather than the class, because construction is where the meaning is: `Fortified` is built with `new Criterion(() => false)` at the call site, `Stowed` builds its own, and `GoTo`'s criterion closes over the unit and its path.

This covers five of the thirteen `Busy` subclasses — `Fortified`, `Fortifying`, `Stowed`, `Sleeping`, `GoTo` — whose criteria are pure functions of the world and the unit, and whose durable facts are saved separately. `Fortify` registers a `Fortified` *`UnitImprovement`* alongside the busy rule, and that is ordinary state.

**It cannot cover the other eight, and the class comment says so rather than leaving someone to find out.** They come from `DelayedAction.perform`, which closes over `endTurn = turn.value() + turns` and the completion `action`. `endTurn` says when the work finishes; `action` says what it does. Neither is derivable from the unit, so a factory would have to invent a completion turn — and a unit three turns into building a road would load either finished or never finishing.

That is the same problem `PendingEffect` exists for: a delayed action *is* "at turn N, do X", which is exactly the handler-plus-data shape 03-save-format.md defines. Darwin's Voyage was taken to be the only unserialisable continuation in the engine. It is one of nine.

`DelayedAction.perform` took a completion callback and now takes a handler identifier. That callback was a closure, and `Unit._busy` — the only field in the engine that holds a `Rule` — held a rule built around it. `core-save-game` refused to encode it, so a unit three turns into building a road could not be saved at all.

`perform` now registers a `PendingEffect` carrying the turn the work comes due, and `delayedBusy` builds the `Busy` rule from *that*. One function, called from two places — `perform` when the action starts and `BusyRegistry` when a save is loaded — because if the two built the rule separately they would drift, and the drift would only appear in a loaded game.

`registerDelayedAction` pairs the two registrations a package needs: the handler that says what finishing does, and the factory that rebuilds the in-progress rule. Split across two call sites they would be easy to half-do, and a package with a handler but no factory produces a unit that loads idle while still owing the work. The action is rebuilt by a factory rather than `new ActionType(...)` because the constructors genuinely differ — `ClearForest` takes a `TerrainFeatureRegistry` where `BuildIrrigation` takes a `Turn`.

**One latent bug fixed on the way.** The criterion compared `turn.value() === endTurn`, so a unit whose completion turn slipped past — a skipped turn, or a save loaded on a later turn — stayed busy for ever with nothing to say why. It is `>=` now, which cannot get stuck and agrees on the turn it is due.
Conformance is unchanged across the nine delayed actions, and a turn-12 save round-trips byte-identically.

**`typeNameOf(Class)`** returns an explicit `static type` when a class declares one and `constructor.name` otherwise, and `idProvider` now keys on it. That rollout is 303 classes across 243 packages, so it is deliberately not a prerequisite for saving.

It reads an *own* `type`, not an inherited one. `static` members are inherited, so `Class.type` on a subclass of a tagged class returns the parent's tag — every descendant of one tagged class would save, load and take ids as that parent, an entity type swallowing a hierarchy. **`idCounters()` / `restoreIdCounters()`** expose the per-class counters a save has to carry. Without them the first entity created after a load takes an id a loaded entity already holds — `City-1` twice, one of them unreachable — and nothing throws. Restoring only ever moves a counter *forward*, because plugin imports create terrain definitions, civilisations and leaders before a save is loaded, and lowering a counter would hand out ids those already hold.

**`ClassRegistry`** maps type name to class for hydration, which allocates with `Object.create(Type.prototype)` and never calls a constructor. It refuses two classes claiming one name, and refuses a name of one character — which is what `keepNames: false` would produce, and saves written then would be unreadable by any other build. §7's explicit tags are the real fix; this makes the failure a startup error instead of a corrupt file. So `inject` has three tables rather than the one the design assumed:

**collaborators** — registries, `turn`, `year`, and the game's `rng` for a `() => number` field. Sixteen entries, two of them spellings of the same thing (`_ruleRegistry` and `_rulesRegistry` both exist).
**caches** — the value the field's own initialiser would have produced: `[]`, `null`, `new Map()`. Five entries.

**derived** — from the game *and* the entity's restored state, so neither table can express them. `Civilization._attributes` is a filtered view of the game's; `World._generator` is rebuilt from the world's own saved height and width, which is exact because every geometry method is a pure function of those two and a loaded world never calls `generate()`.

**The assertion at the end matters more than the tables.** A transient field added later and not added here leaves `undefined` behind, so `inject` throws naming the class and the field. That is what turns the next `Yield` into a load failure instead of a wrong answer.

Four things here differ from the document, each for a reason:

**`ClassRegistry` lives in `core-data-object`.** The layout in the plan puts it here while `hydrate` reads it as `game.classes`, which would make `core-game` depend on this package — and this package depends on `core-game`.

**`SerialisedEntity` carries `keys` beside `id`.** `_keys` is built by `addKey()` calls inside constructors, so no `Game` can supply it, and without it `toPlainObject()` throws and a loaded game sends the renderer nothing. Putting it in `state` instead would mean removing `_keys` from `DataObject.transient`, moving the conformance checksum for something that is bookkeeping rather than state.

**Registry dispositions are exhaustive at compile time.** `registries.ts` types its table as `Record<keyof GameSlots, Disposition>`, so adding a slot to `Game` fails to compile here until someone says whether it is saved. The classifications come from measuring a real game rather than reading names: `terrainFeatures` reads like a mixed registry and is not — its definitions are classes in `availableTerrainFeatures` and every entry is a placed instance. `save` additionally refuses a `state` registry that turns out to hold a class, and `hydrate` refuses membership for a slot that is not state, because loading it would register duplicates over the definitions plugin imports already created.

Stage 3 of the engine serialisation plan, and the piece that unlocks the rest of it: multiplayer, test isolation, and loading a save into a fresh context rather than mutating the running game.

`Game` holds the 43 registries plus turn, year and the random number generator. The dependency injection it needs already existed — every class and every rule factory in the engine takes its registries as constructor parameters with singleton defaults. What was missing was something to pass.

`defaultGame` adopts the existing singletons instead of constructing its own. That is deliberate and it is what makes the migration incremental: while some packages still import `instance` and others take a `Game`, both must see the same registry. Otherwise a half-migrated engine disagrees with itself, and that failure looks like a rule not firing rather than like an error.
Two departures from the plan's sketch, both forced:

It sketched `core-city` re-exporting `defaultGame.cities` as its `instance`, which would make every registry package depend on `core-game` — a cycle. Adoption runs the dependency the other way and needs no change to the registry packages at all.

It also implied every registry in the tree. `civ1-earth-generator`'s two are excluded: baking a specific ruleset into core is wrong, and it would drag `canvas` in with it. What remains is 43, which is the count 01-constraints.md reached independently.

A ruleset's own context — `civ1-game` — subclasses `Game` and adds its registries. Constructing it with only its own slots silently gives it *fresh* core registries rather than the adopted singletons, so it would disagree with every unmigrated package about what the city registry is.
`defaultSlots` makes the fix obvious at the call site: `new Game({ ...defaultSlots, ...mine })`.

`Engine` carries the event stream a game runs on — `turn:start`, `player:turn-end` and the rest. Two games sharing one would each see the other's turns start, which makes it per-game state as much as any registry.

It is also the last parameter type the rule factories take that had no slot: across the seventeen packages with a `registerRules.ts`, 86 factories take 25 distinct parameter types, and with this one every single one maps to a `Game` slot. That is what makes the migration mechanical rather than a judgement per factory.

Two bugs in this repo's own tooling, both found by the conformance suite going silent rather than by anything failing:

`civ sync` preserved each package's `main` entrypoint — `buildPluginList` needs it to exist — but never refreshed it. Excluding a file from deletion is not the same as keeping it current. `node_modules` was serving a `core-game/index.js` from before `defaultSlots` was exported, so `defaultSlots` came back `undefined`, `civ1-game`'s `defaultGame` silently built its own registries instead of adopting the singletons, and `civ1-world`'s rules — including the one that builds the world — registered somewhere nothing would ever read. The codemod was not idempotent: re-run over an already-migrated file it found the new `game.rules.register(...)` call and rewrote its parent again, emitting `export const register = export const register = ...`. A rollout across seventeen packages gets re-run after any one of them fails, so it now detects its own output and skips.

`--pending` deliberately operates on packages the manifest no longer lists — a stage drops them once its work is done — so `manifest.packages[name]` was `undefined` and `resolution` with it. That read as "not github", and `simple-world-generator`, which has never been on npm and is consumed straight from its default branch, was offered to `npm publish` as a new scoped package. npm refused with E402 because scoped packages default to restricted; on an account with a paid plan it would have quietly created a private package. Resolution now comes from the installed tree, which cannot go stale that way.
The second is subtler. npm has two near-identically worded conflicts:
Cannot publish over the previously published versions   — already done Cannot publish over previously staged version           — did NOT finish

Matching loosely on "cannot publish over" treated the second as success, so `core-civ-client@0.1.2` was reported published, tagged and pushed while the registry had only 0.1.1. It finalised on its own a few minutes later, but the tool had already moved on and would not have retried. Staged now raises, saying what it means and that a re-run is safe.

`civ1-city-improvement`'s suite fails 2-3 tests per run, and 6 before Stage 2 touched it — RNG-dependent build-availability assertions, and `WorkedTileRegistry` singleton state leaking between tests. Neither is Stage 2's to fix, and refusing on them means the package can never ship again.

It is recorded in the gate with its reason rather than passed as a flag, so it is visible in review and hard to forget. The suite still runs and the failure is still reported — as a skip, never as a pass — and nothing goes on the list without first checking it fails identically at the commit before the change.

The manifest reports work *remaining*, so when a stage's codemod lands its packages drop out of that stage's set — taking the wave mapping with them and leaving `civ publish --wave N --stage 2` with nothing to publish. That is correct as a description of remaining work and useless as a publish plan, and it bit once per stage.

`--pending` asks the checkouts instead: anything with commits its remote does not have, a version the registry does not have, or no upstream at all (a package a stage introduced). It orders them into waves from the live dependency graph, so `core-random` publishes before the eighteen packages that now depend on it without anyone maintaining a list.

The conformance harness now seeds `@civ-clone/core-random`'s instance instead of overriding `Math.random` globally. The override worked, but it could not survive Stage 3 — two `Game`s in one process would share it — and it could only ever prove the *harness* was deterministic, not that the engine had stopped using the global.

So `Math.random` is instrumented rather than replaced: every call is counted and the count goes in the snapshot, where a non-zero value is a visible failure. It reads 0 at turns 1, 10 and 50. Grepping the source cannot show that, because it cannot see what a dependency resolves to at runtime.

The count sits outside the checksum, alongside the DTO digest, for the same reason: the checksum answers "is the engine state the same", and adding an instrument should not change the number it exists to watch. It did on the first run, which is how the boundary got drawn.

With that, Stage 2 leaves every checksum identical — 7d6b6b04 / 73a0cc05 / 3431063b, as before Stage 1 — and seed 2 still produces the same three checksums it produced before any of this started. Nineteen packages moved off `Math.random` and the draw sequence did not shift.

localChanges: Wave 0 published `core-registry@0.1.2` successfully, and then every way of checking said it had not: `npm view` and the registry's package document are both served from a cache that can lag minutes behind a publish. The only straight answer came from trying to publish again, which said "cannot publish over the previously published versions".

So the pre-check now asks for the exact version rather than the version list — the least stale answer available — and is treated as a hint rather than proof. The conflict itself is read as success, because a stale "not published" on the fourth of twenty packages would otherwise abort the wave half-done.

The first real publish stopped at npm's `EOTP`: this account has two-factor authentication on writes. `npm version patch` had already run, so `core-registry` was left with a local `0.1.2` commit and tag, unpublished and unpushed — recoverable, but only because nothing had been pushed yet.
A retry would have bumped it again, skipping `0.1.2` and leaving that tag pointing at something never published. So `release` is now idempotent:
the tag `npm version` writes is the record that the bump has happened, so a version already bumped is not bumped again
a version already on the registry is not republished

`--otp CODE` passes a 2FA code through. One code covers one publish before its thirty-second window closes, so a wave of twenty needs either an automation token or 2FA set to authorisation-only; `civ publish` says so rather than failing part-way through a wave.
`--dry-run` now reads the live checkout rather than the recorded manifest version, so it cannot claim a package is about to move to the version it is already on.
All twelve waves pass `civ publish --wave N --dry-run`; verify-stage1 reports 0 of 62 needing attention. Nothing is published or pushed.
Also records two findings from getting there:

`core-city`'s suite had been failing deterministically since 2022 — it asserted a city works one tile, when nothing in that package creates a `WorkedTile`, so it was reading whatever the shared registry singleton happened to hold. Fixed in core-city's own `test:` commit.

The first attempt at that fix appeared to do nothing, because a committed `tests/lib/setUpCity.js` sat beside the edited `.ts` and ts-node resolves the `.js`. Same trap as 04-package-workflow.md §1, one level down, and worth stating plainly: a compiled file beside edited source is the first explanation to reach for when an edit seems to have no effect.
Six ways the gate refused a package that was fine, all found by dry-running all twelve waves before publishing anything:

Untracked files counted as a dirty tree. Every untracked file in this tree is a lockfile; npm never packs `package-lock.json`, and the packages carrying a stray `pnpm-lock.yaml` are all GitHub-resolved and so produce no tarball. They are now reported beside the result instead of refused.

A forced rebuild always changes the tree, because the committed `.js` are single-quoted, current `tsc` emits double, and `prettier:format` globs only `**/*.ts` so it never reformats them. "Did the tree change" cannot tell that from genuine staleness. The gate now tests for what staleness actually looks like — compiled output still carrying TypeScript's private-field WeakMap helpers — and reports the reformatting as a note.

The compile was not forced, so `tsc --build` skipped whenever its outputs were newer than its inputs. A skipped compile is indistinguishable from a successful one, which is how five packages came to hold compiled output that had never matched their source.
`core-strategy`'s suite is flaky by construction and failed the gate on a coin flip. It now retries before refusing.

Five packages declare a `ts-mocha` test script without listing `ts-mocha` in devDependencies, so their suites have never been runnable. A missing runner is now detected by looking for the binary rather than by reading an error, and reported as a skip — never as a pass.
`simple-ai-client` cannot be installed at all (its ~20 `github:` dependencies each spawn a nested install, recursively), so it falls back to the renderer's own tsc and prettier.
The checks also restore the checkout when they finish, so `npm publish` packs what the commit and the tag hold rather than the output of the check that just ran.
Stage 0 of docs/engine-serialisation/05-engine-plan.md, plus everything Stage 1 needed in order to be provable.

tools/civ — audit, clone, sync, watch, collisions, check-dts, publish. `audit` recomputes the whole picture from node_modules rather than trusting a hand-maintained list, and reproduces 04-package-workflow.md's table exactly: 325 installed, 22 resolved from GitHub, 62 packages carrying 282 `#private` declarations across 12 publish waves, 17 `registerRules.ts`, 19 packages calling `Math.random`, one three-package dependency cycle.
tools/codemod/private-fields.js — the ts-morph codemod. It also walks class expressions, because `getClasses()` returns declarations only and `core-unit-transport` builds its `Transport` as a mixin.
tools/stage1.js — the per-package procedure. It records what was already failing before it touches anything, so a package that never compiled is reported rather than blamed on the change.
tools/verify-stage1.js — the sweep that catches a commit whose `.js` predates its `.ts`, which is what a silently skipped compile leaves behind.

tests/engine/ — the conformance suite. A seeded four-player game to turn 50 in 11 seconds, recording engine state checksums and, separately, the size and hash of what `toPlainObject()` emits. Separately because Stage 1 leaves the first identical and moves the second; see fixtures/NOTES.md.
tests/engine/hydration.ts — `Object.assign(Object.create(City.prototype), state).name()` returning a value. The point of the whole stage.

Both bundle with esbuild rather than running under ts-node: node resolution finds each package's compiled `.js` first, so a plain require would test the published artifact instead of the source `civ sync` just wrote.

Update to add `status` property to capture the current action being performed (if any) and add in `player` and `visibility` keys for data transfer.
Updates to call `Created` `Rule`s after setting the keys.
Update to use new `Buildable` class from core-city-build.
Ensure `Moved` `Rule`s are triggered at the end of the `DelayedAction` too.
Allow custom `Busy` `Rule`s to be supplied to `DelayedAction`s.
Include the `Action` in `Defeated` `Rule`s so when a `Unit` in a `City` is `Destroyed` it's easy enough to work out if it was a defender.
Track `destroyed` status rather than unregister the `Unit`.
Add event to trigger when `Wonder`s are obsoleted.
Add utilities to help when map data is used elsewhere.
Add `PickGenerator` (to choose the `Generator` to build the `World` map) and `PickStartTile` (to choose the starting `Tile`s for the `Player`) `Rule`s.
Ensure `undefined` is never added to a `Yield`.
Fix caching issue when `Yield`s get modified after caching.
Fix a bug when `Tile` `Yield`s exist for which weights are not provided.
Convert `World` from a `Registry` to a `DataObject` to allow `height` and `width` to be passed to the `Client`.
Have `World#build` return `Promise<World>` to help with tests in other packages.
Fix bug where all `Tile`s were rated as `0` since the changes to `Yield`s.
Update to use more appropriately named iterator type from `core-registry`.
Ensure `RuleRegistry` is passed into `World`s constructor, instead of when used by `build`.
Remove `YieldValue` value object, the high usage combined with `ulid` from `DataObject` was causing slowdowns and didn't need to be a `DataObject` at all.
Add `NegativeYield` as a convenience object for costs.
Prevent infinite loop and output debug info.
Updates to prevent TypeScript being sad about the `catch (e)`, `reject(e)` flow.
Add methods for catching when `City`s or `Unit`s are captured or defeated.
Fix `SimpleAIClient` to use the new `CityBuild` mechanism.
Add hard-coded check for `Earth` map to ensure first `City` is built in the right place.

The moment when, after many years

of hard work and a long voyage

you stand in the centre of your room,

house, half-acre, square mile, island, country,

knowing at last how you got there,

and say, I own this,

        

is the same moment when the trees unloose

their soft arms from around you,

the birds take back their language,

the cliffs fissure and collapse,

the air moves back from you like a wave

and you can't breathe.



No, they whisper. You own nothing.

You were a visitor, time after time

climbing the hill, planting the flag, proclaiming.

We never belonged to you.

You never found us.

It was always the other way round.
